units.title: Unit 19 — Shops and shopping
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 19, printed pages 44–45 (PDF pages 45–46); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: The butcher sells fresh meat.
items.note: A butcher is a person who sells meat. In British English, the shop is commonly called the butcher’s.

items.example: I need to go to the butcher’s.
items.note: The possessive ending is used in the name of the shop: the butcher’s.

items.example: You can buy stamps at the post office.
items.note: You can buy stamps and send letters or parcels at a post office.

items.example: We do our weekly shopping at the supermarket.
items.note: A large self-service shop selling food and other household items.

items.example: There is a bookshop near my office.
items.note: A shop where books are sold; bookstore is common in American English.

items.example: The baker makes fresh bread every morning.
items.note: A baker is a person who makes or sells bread. The shop is usually called the baker’s.

items.example: I bought some rolls at the baker’s.
items.note: In British English, the baker’s means the shop, not a plural group of bakers.

items.example: This department store sells clothes and furniture.
items.note: A large shop divided into departments selling different kinds of goods.

items.example: Ask the chemist about this medicine.
items.note: In British English, a chemist can be a pharmacist; the shop is the chemist’s.

items.example: You can get aspirin at the chemist’s.
items.note: A British English term for a pharmacy. In American English, pharmacy or drugstore is usual.

items.example: The newsagent opens early.
items.note: A person who sells newspapers and magazines; the shop is often called the newsagent’s.

items.pt: banca de jornais; loja de jornais e revistas
items.example: She bought a magazine at the newsagent’s.
items.note: A shop selling newspapers, magazines and often other small items.

items.pt: loja de presentes; loja de lembranças
items.example: The museum has a small gift shop.
items.note: A shop selling presents, souvenirs and small gifts.

items.example: You can buy a beach ball at the toy shop.
items.note: A shop selling toys. This phrase is reinforced in exercise 19.1.

items.example: The restaurant is on the fourth floor.
items.note: In British English, the ground floor is at street level; the first floor is above it.

items.example: The food department is in the basement.
items.note: The level below the ground floor. A department store may have a basement food department.

items.example: Beauty products are on the ground floor.
items.note: In British English, this is the level at street level, below the first floor.

items.example: The women’s clothes are on the first floor.
items.note: In British English, the first floor is above the ground floor. In American English, the first floor is often at street level.

items.example: The children’s department is on the second floor.
items.note: In a British department store, this floor is two levels above the ground floor.

items.example: Furniture is on the third floor.
items.note: The third floor is three levels above the British ground floor.

items.example: The toy section is on the fourth floor.
items.note: The fourth floor is four levels above the British ground floor.

items.example: We bought a sofa in the furniture department.
items.note: An uncountable noun: say some furniture or a piece of furniture, not furnitures.

items.example: Men’s wear is on the second floor.
items.note: A department-store label for clothing for men.

items.example: The children’s department sells baby clothes.
items.note: A section of a department store selling clothes or goods for children.

items.example: Women’s wear is on the first floor.
items.note: A department-store label for clothing for women.

items.example: I bought beauty products downstairs.
items.note: Products such as make-up and skincare items; the store plan also uses the label Beauty.

items.example: You can find a TV in electricals.
items.note: A British shop label for electrical and electronic goods, such as televisions.

items.example: Let’s have lunch in the department store restaurant.
items.note: A place in the department store where customers can eat.

items.example: The toys are on the top floor.
items.note: The plural of toy. The store plan lists Toys on the fourth floor.

items.example: The sign says the shop is open.
items.note: On a shop sign, open means customers may enter and shop.

items.example: The shop is closed on Sunday.
items.note: On a shop sign, closed means the shop is not open for customers.

items.example: Please pay at the cash desk.
items.note: The place in a shop where you pay; cash means money, not the payment counter.

items.example: Push the door to enter.
items.note: On a door sign, push means move the door away from you.

items.example: Pull the door towards you.
items.note: On a door sign, pull means move the door towards you.

items.example: A shop assistant helped me find my size.
items.note: A shop assistant helps customers and handles sales in a shop.

items.example: The customer asked for a different colour.
items.note: A person who buys goods or services from a shop.

items.example: The assistant asked, “Can I help you?”
items.note: A polite offer of assistance often used by a shop assistant.

items.example: Can I try on this jacket?
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: try a jacket on or try it on, not try on it.

items.example: Do you have this in a bigger size?
items.note: Clothes can be a particular size, such as small, medium or large.

items.example: I need a bigger size, please.
items.note: Use a bigger size when a garment is too small for you.

items.example: Have you got a smaller size?
items.note: Use a smaller size when a garment is too big for you.

items.example: Could I see this in a different colour?
items.note: Colour is the British spelling; color is the American spelling.

items.example: Have you got a different colour?
items.note: A common British English question used to ask whether a shop has something available. Supply a specific object when speaking.

items.example: This one is perfect. I’ll take it.
items.note: A natural way to tell a shop assistant that you have decided to buy something.

items.example: How much does that coat cost?
items.note: Use this question to ask the price of one item; for several items, ask How much do they cost?

items.example: Can I pay by cheque here?
items.note: Cheque is the British spelling; check is the American spelling for this means of payment.

items.example: She paid by credit card.
items.note: A card used to buy things with credit rather than immediately using money in your bank account.

items.example: I usually pay with a debit card.
items.note: A card generally used to pay directly from money held in a bank account.

items.example: Can I pay in cash?
items.note: Money in notes and coins. Say pay in cash or pay cash.

items.example: Can I pay by card?
items.note: A useful additional payment phrase; also say pay with a card.

items.example: I only have a twenty-pound note.
items.note: Here, a note means paper money, as in a twenty-pound note; it can also mean a short written message.

items.example: Have you got change for a ten-pound note?
items.note: Here, change means coins or smaller notes returned after paying more than the price.

items.example: Keep the receipt in case you return it.
items.note: A receipt is proof of payment. The letter p in receipt is silent.

items.example: Would you like a carrier bag?
items.note: A British English term for a bag used to carry purchases home.

items.example: The assistant put the shirt in a bag.
items.note: A shop assistant may ask whether you would like a bag for your purchase.

items.example: Where can I pay for this?
items.note: Pay for something means give money in exchange for it; pay by card or pay in cash describes the method.

items.example: I bought two greeting cards at the newsagent’s.
items.note: Cards sent to people on occasions such as birthdays; pictured in exercise 19.1.

items.example: I need to buy some stamps at the post office.
items.note: Postage stamps are mentioned in exercise 19.2.

items.example: She went to the newsagent’s to buy a newspaper.
items.note: A newspaper is one of the items sold by a newsagent; reinforced in exercise 19.2.

learningObjectives: Identify common shops and match them to everyday goods and services.
Find departments in a department store and distinguish the British ground floor, first floor and basement.
Understand common shop and door signs: open, closed, cash desk, push and pull.
Ask for another size or colour, try clothes on, and complete a purchase using natural shop expressions.
Distinguish cash, notes, change, receipts, credit cards and debit cards, and use appropriate payment phrases.

units.title: Unit 20 — Online shopping
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 20, printed pages 46–47 (PDF pages 47–48); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: My sister often shops online.
items.note: Shop can be a verb meaning buy things; online describes shopping on the Internet.

items.example: Online shopping saves me time.
items.note: Buying goods or services over the Internet.

items.example: You can search products by name.
items.note: A shop website may have a Search products box. You can also say search for a product.

items.example: Search for a good price before buying.
items.note: Use search for when looking for a particular thing: search for a website or search for the best price.

items.example: I ordered a white T-shirt.
items.note: A casual shirt with short sleeves; it is also written T-shirt in the source.

items.example: The shop sells T-shirts and tops.
items.note: A general word for upper-body clothes, such as shirts and blouses.

items.example: She bought a warm jumper online.
items.note: In British English, a warm knitted top; sweater is common in American English.

items.example: These trousers are too long.
items.note: Usually plural: these trousers; a pair of trousers.

items.example: I need a new pair of jeans.
items.note: Usually plural: a pair of jeans, not a jean in ordinary clothing descriptions.

items.example: The website has shoes in many sizes.
items.note: A plural form; for one shoe, use shoe.

items.example: These boots are good for winter.
items.note: Shoes that cover the foot and at least part of the ankle or leg.

items.example: He added a jacket to his basket.
items.note: A short coat-like garment worn over other clothes.

items.example: I ordered a new winter coat.
items.note: Outer clothing worn over other clothes, often for warmth.

items.example: I bought the coat in the sale.
items.note: A sale often means goods are offered at lower prices; the word also means an act of selling.

items.example: There are three items in my basket.
items.note: An online shopping basket holds the items you have selected but not yet bought.

items.example: Click here to add the shoes to your basket.
items.note: The usual shopping-site command for putting an item into your online basket.

items.example: Choose the colour you want.
items.note: The British spelling; color is the American spelling.

items.example: Select your size before paying.
items.note: Select a size that fits; the example shop shows small, medium and large.

items.example: Check the price before you order.
items.note: The amount of money an item costs.

items.example: Delivery normally takes four days.
items.note: The act of bringing purchased goods to an address.

items.example: The website offers two delivery options.
items.note: Different delivery services or speeds offered by a seller.

items.example: We chose free delivery.
items.note: Delivery without an additional delivery charge.

items.example: Next day delivery costs five pounds extra.
items.note: A service intended to deliver goods the next day. Check the actual promised date and conditions.

items.example: The delivery charge is five pounds.
items.note: An additional amount paid for delivery; this is a pedagogical extension.

items.example: I read a review before ordering.
items.note: Here, a review means a customer’s opinion or evaluation of a product.

items.example: I read online reviews before I choose a product.
items.note: Customer reviews shown on a website can help buyers compare products.

items.example: I read the reviews before buying anything online.
items.note: Read is pronounced /riːd/ in the present but /red/ in the past.

items.example: Your order will arrive on Friday.
items.note: As a noun, an order is a request to buy goods; as a verb, to order is to request goods for purchase.

items.example: You can see the total under your order.
items.note: A label showing what you have chosen to buy and the details of the purchase.

items.example: Please tell me your order number.
items.note: A reference identifying a purchase; do not confuse it with the delivery address or post code.

items.example: Enter your address at checkout.
items.note: The final stage of an online purchase; the related verb is check out (two words).

items.example: I clicked “delete this item” by mistake.
items.note: A shop-site instruction that removes a selected item from your basket or order.

items.example: Delete the extra item before paying.
items.note: Delete means remove something, for example an unwanted item from your online basket.

items.example: There are two items in the basket.
items.note: One product or thing on a shopping list or in an order.

items.example: The total is sixteen pounds.
items.note: The complete amount to pay for all items and any applicable charges.

items.example: Please check your delivery address.
items.note: The address where goods should be delivered; it may be different from a billing address.

items.example: Enter your full address here.
items.note: A location identified by information such as house number, street, city and post code.

items.example: Write your house number before the street name.
items.note: A number identifying a building on a street.

items.example: She lives on King Street.
items.note: A road in a town or city, often used as part of an address.

items.example: Enter your city and country.
items.note: The town or city part of a delivery address.

items.example: Our UK post code contains both letters and numbers.
items.note: A British post code contains letters and numbers. In American English, the equivalent is a zip code.

items.example: Enter your US zip code to continue.
items.note: An American English term for the numerical postal code; the British equivalent is post code.

items.example: Choose your country from the list.
items.note: A country name forms part of an international delivery address.

items.example: I entered my phone number at checkout.
items.note: A telephone contact number entered on an order form.

items.example: The company sent a receipt by email.
items.note: An email address can be used to send confirmations and updates about an order.

items.example: I paid with a credit card.
items.note: A card used to pay for goods and services on credit.

items.example: You can pay with a credit card online.
items.note: Use with to name the means of payment; pay by credit card is also natural.

items.example: Ordering online is quick and easy.
items.note: A phrase describing something that does not take much time or effort.

items.example: Reviews help me choose what to buy.
items.note: Choose what to buy means decide which item or items you want to purchase.

items.example: I stayed at home to receive a delivery.
items.note: Be at the destination to accept goods when they arrive.

items.word: take it to the post office
items.example: They will take the parcel to the post office.
items.note: In the source, this happens when nobody is at home to receive a delivery.

items.example: I am waiting for a delivery today.
items.note: Use wait for + noun: wait for a delivery, not wait a delivery.

items.example: The parcel was delivered yesterday.
items.note: The past participle of deliver; used in passive forms such as was delivered.

items.example: I called customer care about my order.
items.note: A department or service that helps customers with questions or problems. The phrase appears in exercise 20.3.

items.example: I found the product on a different website.
items.note: A set of web pages at an Internet address; online shops are accessed through websites.

items.example: I didn’t want to pay for delivery.
items.note: Use pay for + service or product; pay by or with + payment method.

items.example: I need a small T-shirt.
items.note: One of the three clothing-size options shown on the shopping page.

items.example: A medium jumper would fit me better.
items.note: A clothing size between small and large, shown in the online shop.

items.example: They only have this coat in large.
items.note: One of the three clothing-size options shown on the shopping page.

learningObjectives: Search for products online and understand size, colour, price, sale labels and customer reviews.
Use online-shop expressions such as add to basket, delete an item, checkout and order number.
Compare free and next-day delivery options, including delivery times and extra costs.
Read and enter delivery details, distinguishing a UK post code from a US zip code.
Describe the steps of an online purchase and ask customer care about a delivery or delayed order.
